Glossary

    Practices in the cloud

    Words: 1164

    Cloud CLIs, polling for readiness, keyless access, API limits, account guardrails, and tag cleanup - and where the boundary with Terraform lies.

    Key idea of this page #

    In the cloud, Bash orchestrates calls to external APIs, where every request costs latency, quota, and money. Four rules define a robust cloud script: explicitly wait for asynchronous resources with a hard attempt limit; never store keys in code or expose them under set -x; batch queries with pagination and API rate limits in mind instead of firing hundreds of calls in a loop; and verify on the very first line which account and region the script targets. Everything created for a task must be discoverable and deletable by tag. The architectural boundary is clear: one-off operations belong in Bash; persistent infrastructure state belongs in Terraform. Triage of live instances and logs is covered separately under SRE practices.

    1 · Cloud CLIs are regular programs and behave like programs #

    The first shift in mindset: a cloud CLI is not an administrative interactive shell, but a CLI utility with an exit status and machine-readable output. The same rules apply to it as to grep.

    aws ec2 describe-instances \
  --filters Name=tag:app,Values=web \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].InstanceId' \
  --output text

aws s3api head-object … >/dev/null 2>&1 \
  && echo exists || echo missing

    When automating cloud CLIs, save time and network bandwidth with two habits. Apply client-side filtering via --query directly before output reaches jq, avoiding megabytes of redundant parsing. Remember that a missing cloud resource returns a non-zero exit code, not an empty string: test command exit codes rather than stdout text. And always disable the built-in pager via AWS_PAGER="" so your script never hangs waiting for you to press q.

    What gets asked: “How does --query differ from jq, and how do you test in a script whether a cloud resource exists?”

    2 · Resource provisioning: waiting is part of the job #

    Cloud calls are asynchronous: returning an ID does not mean the resource is ready. A script that does not wait fails intermittently and manifests as a flaky bug.

    id=$(aws ec2 run-instances … \
     --query 'Instances[0].InstanceId' \
     --output text)

aws ec2 wait instance-running \
  --instance-ids "$id"

# custom polling with an attempt limit
for i in {1..30}; do
  ready && break
  sleep 5
done

    When awaiting infrastructure readiness, use native CLI commands (wait) wherever available. Where absent, write polling loops with strict attempt limits and timeouts so a hung resource never burns your CI runner quota. And immediately tag everything you create: tags ensure you can reliably discover and delete temporary resources later.

    What gets asked: “How do you wait for cloud resource readiness in a script, and what happens without polling?”

    3 · Credentials: what must never appear in scripts #

    The costliest mistakes in cloud scripting are disciplinary rather than technical - credentials leaked into a repository or CI log.

    # no:
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=AKIA…

# yes: instance role or named profile
aws --profile prod s3 ls

# secrets from a vault into a variable,
# never echoed and never under set -x
token=$(aws secretsmanager \
  get-secret-value --secret-id t \
  --query SecretString --output text)

    Configure cloud authentication following a strict hierarchy: instance roles or OIDC relieve you of storing static credentials, while named profiles keep tokens in your user configuration away from code. Leave environment variables strictly as a last resort. And never enable set -x tracing in steps handling authentication: it will print argument values and expose your secrets in CI logs for all to see.

    What gets asked: “How does a script access cloud APIs without storing static credentials, and why is set -x dangerous there?”

    4 · Pagination, API throttling, and avoiding CLI loops #

    Invoking a cloud CLI in a for loop across hundreds of resources guarantees hitting ThrottlingException (Rate exceeded) and inflating runtime to thirty minutes: each invocation boots a Python/Go runtime and establishes a new TLS handshake.

    # no: N API calls in a loop
for id in $ids; do
  aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids "$id"
done

# yes: single batch request with adaptive retries
export AWS_RETRY_MODE=adaptive
export AWS_MAX_ATTEMPTS=6
aws ec2 describe-instances \
  --instance-ids $ids

    Two rules for scale: pass IDs as batches or apply server-side API filters instead of iterative queries, and enable built-in adaptive retries (AWS_RETRY_MODE=adaptive) to automatically back off upon receiving 429 or 503 responses. When querying large listings, remember that without autopagination or --next-token, only the first page is returned.

    What gets asked: “Why do cloud scripts suddenly fail with Rate Exceeded errors, and how do you eliminate CLI loops?”

    5 · Guardrails against the wrong account, region, or context #

    The most destructive cloud outages occur when a valid cleanup script runs in a terminal retaining yesterday's production profile or cluster context.

    #!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

export AWS_PAGER=""
region="${AWS_REGION:?specify region}"
want_acc="123456789012"

got_acc=$(aws sts get-caller-identity \
  --query Account --output text)
[ "$got_acc" = "$want_acc" ] || {
  echo "wrong account: $got_acc" >&2
  exit 1
}

    Any script modifying or deleting cloud resources must in its first lines verify the active account and cluster against expectations (aws sts get-caller-identity, gcloud config get-value project, kubectl config current-context) and require explicit region parameters rather than inheriting stale environment variables from an engineer's shell.

    What gets asked: “How do you ensure a staging cleanup script never touches production resources?”

    6 · Cleanup and the boundary with Terraform #

    Clouds bill for forgotten resources. A script that provisions must be capable of tearing down - identifying targets by metadata tags rather than mental lists.

    aws ec2 describe-instances \
  --filters Name=tag:tmp,Values=yes \
  --query '…[].InstanceId' --output text \
  | xargs -r aws ec2 terminate-instances \
      --instance-ids

    When you pipe cloud resource IDs to deletion commands, always include xargs -r. Without the -r flag, an empty input stream invokes the deletion command with no arguments, and depending on the tool you risk either breaking your script or accidentally terminating all resources in your account.

    Where the boundary lies. Bash excels when the task is an action: ephemeral one-hour setups, account-wide auditing snapshots, bucket migrations, tag-based cleanups. Terraform and CloudFormation excel when the task is state: resources that must exist permanently. A script attempting state management inevitably degenerates into a defective Terraform clone - complete with custom state files, hand-rolled drift detection, and unique bugs.

    What gets asked: “Where does provisioning via shell script end and Terraform begin?”

    Artifacts: what you take away from this page #

    Reading >> Your life quantum · Dignity partnership with AI · Rewiring your neural network

    Account validation at the entrypoint and tag-based cleanup at exit. Your time was well spent if you stopped looping cloud CLI calls one resource at a time, and now begin every script by confirming account identity and every temporary resource with a tracking tag. That is the essence of rewiring: the cloud ceases to be a minefield of surprise billing and mistaken regions.

    1. CLI as a standard program: exit status, client-side --query, disabling AWS_PAGER.
    2. Explicit readiness polling via wait or bounded loops.
    3. Credential hierarchy: instance roles or OIDC → named profiles → environment variables; strict prohibition of set -x with secrets.
    4. Batch requests and AWS_RETRY_MODE=adaptive instead of per-item CLI loops.
    5. Account and region validation on line one before executing any mutating operations.
    6. Tag-based cleanup, xargs -r, and the architectural boundary: actions in Bash, state in Terraform.
